meaning: Union, yoking — spiritual and ascetic discipline by which the individual self is joined to the divine; also the name of one of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy.

phonemes.desc: From √yuj, “to yoke, join”; the o is long — the yoking of the self to the divine.
The abstract noun: the yoking itself — the discipline by which union is achieved.

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: iugum, English “yoke” — the same Indo-European root

pronunciation.note: The word and English “yoke” are cousins: yoga is the yoke worn willingly. The root √yuj also yields English "yoke" — the cognate pair has named the same joining for five millennia.

domains.title: Union, the Yoking of Self to Divine
domains.subtitle: The Discipline That Joins
domains.lead: Yoga is the discipline of union: the yoking — the same root as English ‘yoke’ — of mind, breath, and self to the still point beneath them. Born in the ascetic experiments of the late Vedic age, codified by Patañjali’s sūtras, it is both one of the six orthodox schools of Indian philosophy and, in the Bhagavadgītā’s teaching, the art of every act done without attachment to its fruit.

cards.name: The Eight Limbs
cards.desc: Patañjali’s aṣṭāṅga: restraint, observance, posture, breath, withdrawal, focus, meditation, absorption.

cards.name: Union of Rivers
cards.desc: The yogin joins mind to breath to object as rivers join the sea — the Upaniṣadic image.

cards.name: Yoga in the Gītā
cards.desc: Skill in action: the yogin works without craving the fruit — karma-yoga as the path for the householder.

cards.name: The Cessation of the Waves
cards.desc: Patañjali’s definition: yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ — the stilling of thought’s waves, so the seer abides in itself.

mythology.lead: Yoga has no myths — it has sūtras, and the sūtras are their own literature of precision. Its ‘stories’ are the doctrine’s own history: the ascetics in the forests of the Upaniṣads, the Nātha-lineage’s wonder-working adepts, and the modern export that made a metaphysical discipline into the world’s most practised physical art.

myths.title: The Chariot Simile
myths.text: The body the chariot, the senses the horses, the mind the reins, the intellect the driver, the rider the self: the Kaṭha Upaniṣad’s simile is the oldest complete map of the psychophysical discipline. Who holds the reins attains the end of the road — ‘the still place from which the wise do not return’.

myths.title: The Yoga of Three Paths
myths.text: The Gītā democratizes the discipline: jñāna-yoga of knowledge for the philosopher, karma-yoga of selfless work for the householder, bhakti-yoga of devotion for the lover of god. ‘Yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi’ — established in yoga, act — is the verse on which Gandhi claimed to have fed his whole life.

myths.title: The One Hundred Ninety-Five Sūtras
myths.text: Patañjali’s Yoga-sūtra — c. 195 aphorisms — systematized what had been experiment: the eight limbs, the afflictions, the meditative absorptions, the supernormal powers that are signs on the path and traps at its end. Commentators from Vyāsa to the present have kept it the living constitution of the discipline.

myths.title: The Immortal Teachers
myths.text: The medieval Nātha order gave yoga its adepts-legend: Matsyendra caught among the fishes, Gorakṣa the miracle-working founder, and later figures claimed to walk the centuries — the siddhas, perfected ones, whose bodies outlast death. Hatha-yoga’s physical canon comes from this line of embodied experimenters.

lore.syncretism: Buddhism and Jainism adopted yoga wholesale — the Buddha’s dhyāna is Patañjali’s dhāraṇā by another name — while Sufi India found its own correspondences. The modern export reversed the flow: haṭha-yoga, stripped of metaphysics, returned to India from the West as physical culture before being re-spiritualized. The word is now claimed by three civilizations at once.
lore.culturalLegacy: Some two hundred million people practise asana today — the largest following of any discipline in the lexicon. ‘Yoga’ entered English as a loan-word a century ago and now needs no italics. The discipline’s texts stand, with the Upaniṣads and the Gītā, among the world’s most translated and most printed books.
lore.extendedMeditation: Yoga: the yoke that joins — and the word itself is joined, across four millennia and two language families, to ‘yoke’. Restored plainly, it demonstrates what the discipline teaches: the simplest form can carry the heaviest joining. Two syllables, one root, half the planet practising.
lore.archaeology: The discipline leaves postures, not temples: the Mohenjo-daro seal of a figure in yogic seat (its identity debated), the Mathura images of śramaṇa ascetics, and the modern globe’s studios. The oldest ‘monument’ is the human body arranged to be still.
lore.cult: No priesthood — the practitioner is the officiant. The daily āsana and prāṇāyāma are the liturgy; the guru is the tradition’s single human institution. International Day of Yoga (June 21) is its largest annual congregation.
lore.iconography: The seated ascetic — Śiva as Yogīśvara, lord of yogis, on the Elephanta reliefs — is the discipline’s master-image: stillness arranged. The cakra-diagrams of the subtle body and the haṭha-yoga’s diagrams of the inner sun and moon are its anatomy.
lore.reception: The modern world received yoga twice: first as esoteric philosophy through theosophy, then as physical culture through the global āsana movement. Scholars debate what was lost and what survived; the practice itself — two hundred million daily acts of stillness — is the largest living answer the lexicon contains.
